{#ljef} # Materials and methods

{#ly6g} ## Acquisition of tissue specimens

{#euii} ⟨待采纳·删除·张教授⟩ The training cohort consisted of 98 patients with advanced ESCC with paraffin-embedded tissue archived at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (Guangzhou, China) between 2002 and 2008. Thirty healthy esophageal mucosa tissue blocks were retrieved as the control. The validation cohort consisted of 46 patients with advanced ESCC receiving treatment at the Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital (Tianjin, China). All tissue specimens were obtained as diagnostic biopsies via esophagoscopy and pathologically confirmed before initiation of any antitumor therapy. All patients received cisplatin-based chemotherapy and concurrent radiotherapy (daily dose of 1.8–2.0 Gy to a total dose of 60–70 Gy over 6–7 weeks). In addition, 10 paired fresh ESCC tissues and adjacent non-neoplastic esophageal mucosa tissues were collected at Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital. ESCC was staged according to the 6th edition of the International Union against Cancer (UICC 2002).

{#lp5u} # Abstract

{#bo9v} **Background: **Cisplatin-based chemotherapy with concurrent radiotherapy is a standard treatment for advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). NS1-binding protein (NS1-BP), a member of the BTB-kelch protein family, has been shown to inhibit the proliferation of Hela cells by suppressing c-Myc. In the present study, we examined the potential function role of NS1-BP expression in ESCC, and particularly, the sensitivity of ESCC to radiotherapy.

{#bb7b} **Methods: **NS1-BP expression was examined using immunohistochemistry in two cohorts (n = 98 for the training cohort; n = 46 for independent validation cohort) of ESCC patients receiving cisplatin-based chemotherapy and concurrent radiotherapy. Normal esophageal mucosal tissue blocks were used as a control. We also conducted a series of in vitro and in vivo experiments to examine the potential effects of over-expressing NS1-BP on ESCC cells, and particularly their sensitivity to ionizing irradiation.

{#dwvo} # Discussion

{#lvt1} ⟨待采纳·删除·张教授⟩ NS1-BP reportedly inhibits pre-mRNA splicing, and regulates influenza A viral gene expression and replication [@w:w18]. However, little is known about its expression and importance in human cancers. In the present study, we demonstrated that NS1-BP downregulation is positively correlated with chemoradiotherapeutic resistance and a shorter DSS. Furthermore, our in vitro and in vivo experiments revealed that ectopic restoration of NS1-BP enhanced ESCC radiosensitivity by suppressing c-Myc signalling at the transcriptional level. Taken together, our findings highlight the fundamental roles of NS1-BP in ESCC, and suggest its potential application as a prognostic predictor of ESCC.

{#nvya} ⟨待采纳·新增·张教授⟩ NS1-BP reportedly inhibits pre-mRNA splicing, and regulates influenza A viral gene expression and replication [@w:w17]. However, little is known about its expression and importance in human cancers. In the present study, we suggested that NS1-BP downregulation is positively correlated with chemoradiotherapeutic resistance and a shorter DSS. ops.markdown: c-Myc regulates 15% of all human genes, and is involved in many biological processes associated with both apoptosis induction and cell-cycle arrest [@w:w27]. As expected, NS1-BP overexpression decreased levels of CDK4 and survivin, downstream c-Myc effectors regulating cell cycle and proliferation, whereas the cell cycle inhibitor p27 increased following c-Myc depletion. Upon IR-induced DNA damage, ATM is rapidly activated by c-Myc and other factors, which in turn activate Chk1 and Chk2 [@w:w28]. Consistently, IR activated both the ATM/Chk1 and ATM/Chk2 pathways in ESCC cells; interestingly, NS1-BP significantly inhibited IR-induced ATM/Chk1 phosphorylation without affecting Chk2 phosphorylation. ATM/Chk1 activation induces both G<sub>1</sub> and G<sub>2</sub>/M arrest, whereas ATM/Chk2 activation mainly induces G<sub>1</sub> arrest. Because the G<sub>1</sub> checkpoint is defective in most cancer cells whereas the G<sub>2</sub> checkpoint is rarely impaired, abrogation of the G<sub>2</sub> checkpoint often sensitizes cancer cells to IR [@w:w29]. Our findings showed that NS1-BP decreased IR-induced G<sub>2</sub>/M arrest by suppressing the c-Myc/ATM/Chk1 pathway, thereby sensitizing ESCC cells to IR. Other c-Myc targets, and molecules other than c-Myc, are also implicated in radiosensitivity. {#ywop} Genetic and epigenetic comparisons of normal tissue and tumor tissues are arguably the most effective way to identify tumor-related genes [@w:w19].
